cards.text: Psalm 136 is a song of thanks to the LORD. It opens with a call to give thanks to Him, and it does NOT make you wait for the reason.

cards.question: Psalm 136 opens by saying to give thanks to the LORD. What reason does it give right away?

cards.text: Right after that comes a line about the LORD's loving devotion. Get comfortable with it, friend, because this line is about to become your roommate.

cards.question: In Psalm 136, how long does the LORD's loving devotion last?

cards.text: 'His loving devotion endures forever.' This song ends EVERY verse with that line, twenty-six times, like a houseguest who moved in, unpacked and changed the Wi-Fi password.
Then the call keeps climbing: "Give thanks to the God of gods." And then, "Give thanks to the Lord of lords."

cards.question: True or false: Psalm 136 says the LORD does great wonders with help from His angels.

cards.text: Then the song rewinds all the way to the beginning. The LORD made the heavens.

cards.question: Psalm 136 says the LORD made the heavens by His ___.
True or false: Psalm 136 says the LORD spread out the earth upon the waters.

cards.text: Then He made the great lights. Friend, I've got a whole night sky over my bakery just sitting there waiting on stars, so I take this one PERSONALLY.

cards.question: Psalm 136 gives each great light a job: the sun to rule the ___, and the moon and stars to govern the ___.

cards.text: Sun on days, moon and stars on nights, and not ONE of them has called in sick. I've had oven timers with worse attendance.

cards.question: So far, Psalm 136 has been thanking the LORD for what?

cards.text: Then the song leaves creation behind and jumps into Israel's own story. Next stop: Egypt.

cards.question: In Egypt, what does Psalm 136 say the LORD struck down?

cards.text: Then He brings Israel out from among them. Right out of Egypt.

cards.question: True or false: Psalm 136 says the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt quietly, with no show of power.

cards.text: Quiet? Friend, it was with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Then comes the Red Sea.

cards.question: At the Red Sea, what does Psalm 136 say the LORD does?

cards.text: And He leads Israel right through the middle. I get nervous walking through a crowded kitchen, and these folks walked through the middle of a SEA.

cards.question: What happens to Pharaoh and his army at the Red Sea in Psalm 136?

answers.text: They are swept into the sea

cards.text: Then He leads His people through the wilderness. The whole wilderness, ONE verse, and I can't tell you about my morning in one verse.
Then the LORD strikes down great kings, mighty kings. And this time the song names names.

cards.question: Psalm 136 names two of the mighty kings the LORD struck down. Who are they?
Psalm 136 says the LORD gave the ___ of those kings as an inheritance to His servant Israel.

cards.text: Then the song changes one little word. It stops saying His servant Israel and starts saying us: He remembered us.

cards.question: True or false: Psalm 136 says the LORD remembered us when we were strong.
After remembering us in our low estate, what does Psalm 136 say the LORD freed us from?

cards.text: Then the song zooms ALL the way out. Not just Israel, not just us, but every creature.

cards.question: Psalm 136 says the LORD gives ___ to every creature.
True or false: Psalm 136 ends the way it began, with a call to give thanks.

cards.text: Last line: "Give thanks to the God of heaven! His loving devotion endures forever." Creation, Egypt, the sea, the wilderness, the kings, every creature, and friend, that line showed up for ALL of it.

findings.problem: The joke compares the psalm's refrain about the LORD's loving devotion to an annoying houseguest who changed the Wi-Fi password. That makes Scripture's refrain the target of the joke. The comparison's action (taking over, being a nuisance) also doesn't match the core action of the fact (repeating at the end of every verse).

rule.text: His humor never targets God, Jesus, Scripture or the Marriage Supper.

findings.problem: The joke's comparison doesn't share the fact's core action. The refrain repeats in every verse. A houseguest who unpacked and changed the Wi-Fi password is about taking over a space, not repeating.

rule.text: The everyday comparison must have the same action.

findings.problem: No story card sets up verse 4. The baker hasn't been told about great wonders, or that the LORD does them alone. Whether angels helped is left to luck.

rule.text: Before each choice card, Papa Dorin's story card gives enough context that the baker can reason their way to the answer.

findings.problem: The blank asks the baker to guess the exact word "insight" against "strength" and "command". Nothing earlier lets the baker reason it out. This tests unseen wording, not meaning.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

findings.problem: The setup joke ties stars to the night sky right before card 12 asks what the moon and stars govern. That points the baker to "night".

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: This story card only repeats verses 8 and 9, which card 12 just covered, as a vehicle for a joke. It doesn't move the baker forward through the passage.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: The card says the song "changes one little word" and "stops saying His servant Israel". It doesn't swap one word. "His servant Israel" appears only once (v22), and verse 23 is a new line that speaks of "us". The noticing isn't true as stated.

rule.text: What he points out must be true. "Same words" means an exact match.

findings.problem: Card 16 sets up "every creature" but gives nothing that points to food over breath or shelter. The blank is a wording guess, not a reasoned pick.

rule.text: The check: could a thoughtful baker who has only seen the earlier cards make a reasoned pick? If the only way to get it right is luck, give the story card more context or ask a different question.
